meta.title: LA County Voter Guide
meta.jurisdiction: City of Los Angeles · LA County · California
meta.ballotNote: Your paper ballot has 5 cards printed front and back (pages 1–9). Fill each circle completely with black or blue ink. You don't have to vote in every contest.
meta.retentionExplainer: Appellate justices are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Commission on Judicial Appointments. Every 12 years (or at the first gubernatorial election after appointment) voters decide whether to keep them — no opponent runs. A YES vote keeps the justice for a new 12-year term; if NO wins, the governor appoints a replacement. California voters have removed justices only once (Chief Justice Rose Bird and two colleagues in 1986). Retention votes are meant to remove judges for serious misconduct or incompetence, not over single rulings.
meta.disclaimer: This guide is independent and non-partisan. Summaries attribute arguments to the people and groups who make them; inclusion of an argument is not an endorsement. Contest order and names were transcribed from a sample of the official ballot (precinct 9001430A) — always check your own ballot and lavote.gov. Research current as of October 6, 2026.

contests.office: Mayor — City of Los Angeles
contests.note: Nonpartisan runoff between the top two finishers in June. Both candidates are Democrats.
contests.about: The mayor runs city departments (LAPD, LAFD, sanitation, planning, etc.), proposes the ~$13B budget, appoints general managers and commissioners, and can veto City Council actions. Four-year term. The winner will oversee preparations for the 2028 Olympics.

candidates.name: Karen Bass
candidates.background: Elected mayor in 2022 — the first woman to hold the job. Previously a U.S. Representative (2011–2022) and Speaker of the California Assembly. Founded the South LA nonprofit Community Coalition in 1990.
stands: Homelessness: declared an emergency on day one and launched Inside Safe, which moves encampment residents into motels/interim housing; her campaign cites a ~17.5% drop in street homelessness in her first two years and 6,000+ people placed indoors.
Wants to dismantle the LA Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) and put homeless services under direct city control.
Housing: Executive Directive 1 fast-tracks 100%-affordable projects; promotes adaptive reuse of offices.
Public safety: appointed Chief Jim McDonnell, supports expanding LAPD (roughly 9,500 officers now) and growing unarmed crisis-response teams; touts crime at a 60-year low.
Olympics: created an Office of Major Events and pledges independent audits so taxpayers aren't left with the bill.
Film jobs: pushing Sacramento for larger film tax credits and appointing a local film liaison.
Immigration: describes her stance toward federal raids as "resistance with a purpose."
criticisms: Palisades Fire: critics, including former candidate Spencer Pratt, fault her for being in Ghana when the January 2025 fire began and for city preparedness (e.g., an empty Santa Ynez reservoir). She has faced reporting that her office sought edits to the LAFD after-action report, which she denies.
She fired Fire Chief Kristin Crowley, who has since filed a wrongful-termination lawsuit.
Raman says Inside Safe is expensive (~$300–400M) and that about 40% of participants returned to homelessness, and criticizes Bass for resisting an independent audit of the program.
Raman argues the 2023 LAPD raise Bass backed helped create a ~$1B budget deficit that cut funding for streetlights, sidewalks and potholes.
Raman says the city lost ~40,000 film jobs under Bass and that only a fraction of ED1's claimed affordable units are actually under construction.
Polls cited by AP and LAist show her unfavorable ratings above 50%.
candidates.endorsements: LA County Democratic Party, LA County Federation of Labor, Los Angeles Police Protective League, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris, Nancy Pelosi, EMILY's List.

candidates.name: Nithya Raman
candidates.background: LA City Councilmember for District 4 (Hollywood Hills, Silver Lake, Sherman Oaks area) since 2020, when she became the first challenger in 18 years to unseat a sitting councilmember. Urban planner; born in India and moved to the U.S. at age 6. Elected with Democratic Socialists of America support. Chaired the council's Housing and Homelessness Committee.
stands: Homelessness: "real accountability" — audit every city homelessness dollar on day one, publish performance dashboards, tie funding to results; would leave LAHSA for a new city homelessness bureau. Cites a ~49–54% drop in encampments in her district and pledges to halve street homelessness citywide by the 2028 Olympics.

Housing: build across every neighborhood; supports implementing state law SB 79 (density near transit) with city guidelines such as unit/height caps. Authored a 4% cap on annual rent increases for rent-stabilized units and touts "the strongest tenant protections in city history."
Basic services: focus on streetlights, sidewalks and potholes; says past contracts created the deficit.
Police: keep the force at its current size, replace Chief McDonnell, and expand unarmed crisis response so officers focus on emergencies.
Film jobs: lobby for a state film tax credit as large as Georgia's or New Jersey's.
Olympics: demands enforceable liability caps; authored LA's sanctuary city ordinance.
Opposes loosening short-term-rental rules for the Olympics, saying it would displace tenants.
criticisms: Bass argues Raman has been at City Hall "twice as long as I have" and chaired the homelessness committee, so she shares responsibility for the problems she criticizes.
Bass credits the drop in District 4 homelessness to Inside Safe, not Raman's own efforts.
Bass and Pratt note Raman voted against expanding anti-camping (41.18) zones.
Bass points to a 2020 social-media post in which Raman expressed support for "defunding the police" and calls her inconsistent on public safety.
Bass says Raman lacks the experience and support to carry out her plans. AP framed the race as a test of whether voters want to move the city further left, given Raman's DSA backing.
candidates.endorsements: Democratic Socialists of America, City Controller Kenneth Mejia, Progressive LA, UNITE HERE Local 11.

contests.office: City Attorney — City of Los Angeles
contests.note: Open seat in practice: incumbent Hydee Feldstein Soto finished third in June. Nonpartisan runoff.
contests.about: The City Attorney is the city's lawyer (defending it in lawsuits, advising the council) AND the prosecutor for misdemeanors committed in LA (e.g., DUIs, petty theft, some gun crimes). Four-year term.

candidates.name: Marissa Roy
candidates.background: California deputy attorney general under Rob Bonta, focused on consumer protection. Earlier worked in the LA City Attorney's office as a fellow, represented LA County in litigation against the first Trump administration, and worked at the Public Rights Project. Monrovia native; 34. Led the June primary with ~43%.
stands: Run the office as a "public interest law firm" — affirmative lawsuits against wage theft and abusive landlords.
Create a dedicated Tenants' Rights Team and significantly increase wage-theft investigators.
"Care-first" approach to homelessness rather than enforcement-led.
Use the office as a legal check on the Trump administration (immigration raids, federal funding).
criticisms: McKinney says her reluctance to enforce the encampment ban and "George Gascón-like" crime policies make her "too extreme and out of touch."
Feldstein Soto called some of her promises "insane" and noted she has little experience defending the city in large civil lawsuits, the office's biggest financial exposure.
The LA Times reported she is backed by a PAC funded partly by lawyers whose firms frequently sue the city.
candidates.endorsements: U.S. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, City Controller Kenneth Mejia, Planned Parenthood Advocacy Project LA County.

candidates.name: John McKinney
candidates.background: LA County prosecutor for nearly 30 years; has tried ~40 murder cases, including the Nipsey Hussle case, and heads the DA's bureau of specialized prosecutions. Ran for District Attorney in 2024. UCLA Law graduate; 58.
stands: Public safety first: tougher prosecution of misdemeanor gun crimes and animal abuse.

"Compassionate accountability" on homelessness: enforce laws against encampments that block the public right-of-way or pose health risks while lining up services, using arrests as leverage into treatment.
Reduce what the city pays out in lawsuits.
criticisms: Roy and others note he has no civil-litigation background, though defending the city in civil suits is a core part of the job.
Roy criticized him for benefiting from ~$1.7M in independent spending by an Airbnb-backed PAC — a company the City Attorney's office sued over alleged wildfire price-gouging.
Critics say his campaign's comparisons of opponents to former DA George Gascón are fear-based.
candidates.endorsements: Los Angeles Police Protective League, LA County DA Nathan Hochman, Councilmember Traci Park.

Pushing back on Trump administration policies affecting California.

candidates.name: Laura Friedman
candidates.ballotOccupation: Member, United States House of Representatives

In Congress, a member of the Democratic minority; her office highlights wildfire recovery and opposition to Trump administration policies.

candidates.name: Scott Alan Meyers
candidates.background: Small business owner. Won 16.6% in June. Raised about $58,000 as of June 30, 2026 versus Friedman's ~$828,000.
stands: Little published platform information; runs as a Republican alternative focused on cost of living.
criticisms: Very limited fundraising and public campaign activity in a district that voted heavily Democratic in recent elections.

contests.title: Property transfer tax exemption for Palisades Fire victims
contests.summary: Gives a one-time exemption (or refund) from the City's Measure ULA "mansion tax" for residential properties damaged or destroyed in the January 2025 Palisades Fire, if the owner on the day of the fire sells between Jan. 7, 2025 and Jan. 6, 2030.
contests.currentLaw: Measure ULA (2022) adds a 4% tax on LA property sales over ~$5.4M and 5.5% over ~$10.9M (inflation-adjusted). Revenue funds affordable housing and tenant assistance. Many burned Palisades lots and homes sell above that threshold.
contests.yesMeans: Fire-damaged residential properties sold within five years by their pre-fire owners skip the ULA tax; taxes already paid get refunded.
contests.noMeans: Those sales keep paying ULA like any other sale over the threshold.
pros: Supporters argue ULA was never meant to penalize people who lost their homes in a disaster and are forced to sell.
Narrow: only pre-fire owners, only verified damaged/destroyed residential properties, only for five years — not a loophole for investors.
Broad bipartisan coalition including the mayor, council president, state legislators and building trades.
cons: The City estimates $35M–$66M less for ULA's affordable housing and homelessness-prevention programs through 2030.
Only sales above ~$5.4M qualify, so the benefit goes to owners of high-value properties, while the lost revenue would have funded programs for low-income renters.
Sets a precedent for future exemptions to a voter-approved tax.
contests.fiscal: No effect on the General Fund. Reduces House LA Fund (ULA) revenue by an estimated $35M–$66M through Jan. 2030.
contests.ballotSupporters: Councilmember Traci Park; Mayor Bass; Council President Harris-Dawson; Western States Carpenters; Palisades Community Council

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: City infrastructure, budget, finance and contracting (charter amendment)
contests.summary: A package of City Charter changes from the Charter Reform Commission: requires a long-term capital infrastructure plan; switches to a two-year budget cycle; gives the Director of Public Works more authority and lets the Council restructure or eliminate the five-member Board of Public Works by ordinance; lets the City mortgage its property and run commercial businesses; exempts certain critical infrastructure projects from competitive bidding rules; and allows minor paperwork errors on bidders' ethics forms to be fixed.
contests.currentLaw: One-year budgets; no required infrastructure plan; Public Works is run by a full-time appointed Board; the City may not mortgage property or run purely commercial businesses.
contests.yesMeans: The charter changes above take effect.
contests.noMeans: Current budget, Public Works and contracting rules stay in place.
pros: Supporters (Controller Mejia, Councilmembers Yaroslavsky and Blumenfield) say LA can't fix billions in deferred street, sidewalk and streetlight repairs without a long-term plan and clear responsibility.
Two-year budgets force leaders to consider future costs.
One accountable Public Works director, still overseen by the Mayor, Council and elected Controller.
Removes outdated restrictions that make it harder to use city assets efficiently.
cons: Councilmember Monica Rodriguez argues it lets the Council eliminate the Board of Public Works — which reviews contracts in public meetings — and concentrate power in one person after years of City Hall corruption scandals.
Exempting some projects from competitive bidding and allowing the City to mortgage property could add financial and corruption risk.
Opponents note a capital plan could be adopted without changing the Charter.
Bundles many unrelated changes into one yes/no vote.
contests.fiscal: $4M–$6M one-time cost to upgrade budget systems and train staff. Effects of the contracting, mortgage and business changes can't be estimated.
contests.ballotSupporters: City Controller Mejia; Councilmembers Yaroslavsky & Blumenfield; former City Controller Galperin; Investing in Place

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: City Planning Department (charter amendment)
contests.summary: Replaces the seven Area Planning Commissions with one citywide Neighborhood Appeals Commission (at least 7 members) that hears planning appeals fresh; sets new procedures and deadlines for the City Council to take over planning decisions; puts Planning Department staff in charge of certain quasi-judicial land-use decisions; treats General Plan amendments as approved if the Council doesn't act within 75 days; and lets the Council change the Charter's density cap (floor area of 13× the lot) by ordinance.
contests.currentLaw: Seven regional Area Planning Commissions hear many appeals; if the Council doesn't act on a General Plan amendment in 75 days it's automatically disapproved; the floor-area cap is fixed in the Charter.
contests.yesMeans: The planning changes above take effect.
contests.noMeans: The current planning structure stays.
pros: Supporters (Charter Reform Commission chair Raymond Meza; Engineers & Architects Association) say clearer rules and fewer politically discretionary decisions reduce opportunities for corruption — several recent City Hall scandals involved land-use favors.
A single, consistent appeals body and professional staff decisions should speed routine approvals and housing.
Saves an estimated $360K a year in commission costs.
cons: No official argument against was filed. A possible concern: the seven regional Area Planning Commissions give each part of the city its own appeals body; one citywide commission may be less locally focused.
Deeming General Plan amendments approved when the Council doesn't act flips the default in favor of change.
Letting the Council raise the density cap by ordinance removes a voter-level check on very tall/dense buildings.
contests.fiscal: Not expected to affect revenue. Commission costs drop by about $360,000/year (from $1.1M to $740K).
contests.ballotSupporters: Raymond Meza, Chair, Charter Reform Commission; Roy Samaan, President, Engineers & Architects Association

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: City ethics, elections and governance (charter amendment)
contests.summary: Strengthens the independence of the LAPD Inspector General and LAFD Independent Assessor to open investigations/audits without their commission's approval; bars Ethics Commissioners and the Ethics director from running for city or LAUSD office for five years after leaving; raises campaign-finance penalties to the greater of $15,000 or 3× the improper amount; reduces the required City Council meetings from three per week to at least one; raises referendum petition signatures from 10% to 15% of the last mayoral vote; and lets Neighborhood Council "stakeholder" be defined by ordinance.
contests.currentLaw: Council must meet three days a week; referendums need signatures equal to 10% of the last mayoral vote; police/fire watchdogs need commission sign-off for some investigations.
contests.yesMeans: The ethics, oversight, meeting and referendum changes above take effect.
contests.noMeans: Current rules stay in place.
pros: Supporters (Councilmembers McOsker, Yaroslavsky, Harris-Dawson, Hernandez) say it gives real independence to police and fire watchdogs and tougher penalties for campaign-finance violations.
Five-year cooling-off period keeps Ethics Commissioners from using the post as a springboard.
Three-meetings-a-week is unusual among big cities; one predictable weekly meeting would free councilmembers to work in their districts.
Possible savings on translation and captioning costs.
cons: Councilwoman Monica Rodriguez argues the ethics reforms are a wrapper for cutting public Council meetings by two-thirds — fewer chances for residents to comment and watch, after years of scandals.
Fewer meetings likely means even fewer Council sessions held in the San Fernando Valley.
Raising referendum signature requirements to 15% makes it harder for residents to challenge Council decisions at the ballot.
Bundles popular and unpopular changes into one vote.
contests.fiscal: Possible General Fund savings from fewer meetings; added costs for police/fire investigators can't be determined.
contests.ballotSupporters: Councilmembers Tim McOsker, Katy Yaroslavsky, Marqueece Harris-Dawson

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: Recreation and Parks budget (charter amendment)
contests.summary: Doubles the guaranteed minimum General Fund budget for the Department of Recreation and Parks — from 0.0325% to 0.065% of the assessed value of city property — phased in over 10 years. No new tax: the money comes out of the existing General Fund. During a declared fiscal emergency the Council can cut the increase by up to 30%, but never below today's floor.
contests.currentLaw: The Charter guarantees Rec & Parks 0.0325% of assessed property value (a formula unchanged since 1937). The department runs 500+ parks, 123 rec/senior centers and 52 pools.
contests.yesMeans: Parks get a guaranteed, growing share of the General Fund, reaching roughly double today's minimum by 2036–37.
contests.noMeans: The current minimum stays; parks funding continues to be set in the annual budget.
pros: Supporters say LA ranks 93rd of 100 big cities in Trust for Public Land's 2026 ParkScore and funds parks two-thirds less than similar cities; facilities need ~$3B in repairs.
Keeps pools, rec centers and senior centers open; restores park staff and rangers; builds parks in underserved areas (1/3 of residents lack a park within a 10-minute walk).
No tax increase; requires annual spending plans reviewed in public.
Health and tourism benefits (supporters cite $11 in health savings per $1 of programming).
cons: No official opposing argument was filed, but the City Administrative Officer warns the money must be shifted from other services — including public safety, public works and homeless services — rising to ~$497M/year more by 2036–37.
Locking a spending formula into the Charter reduces flexibility for future mayors and councils during a period of ~$1B deficits.
Ballot-box budgeting: other departments may seek similar set-asides.
contests.fiscal: No new revenue. Increases Rec & Parks' guaranteed funding from ~$303M to ~$995M by 2036–37 (about $32M more in year one, $497M more in year ten), reducing what's available for other city services.
contests.ballotSupporters: LA City Councilmembers Monica Rodriguez, Imelda Padilla & Ysabel Jurado; LA City Controller Kenneth Mejia; Father Greg Boyle
contests.otherSupport: LA Waterkeeper, LA Neighborhood Land Trust, LA Parks Foundation, Boys & Girls Club of SFV

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: City Airports, Harbor, and Water & Power departments (charter amendment)
contests.summary: Lets the City approve leases up to 66 years (from 50) for the Airports department (LAWA) and DWP; requires three Airport Commissioners from the LAX area and two from the Van Nuys Airport area (up from one each); writes into the Charter the Port's practice of spending 10% of operating income (~$28.6M/yr) on waterfront public-access projects; and requires applicants for certain Port leases and coastal permits to disclose effects on jobs.
contests.currentLaw: 50-year max leases for LAWA/DWP (66 for the Port); one LAX-area and one Van Nuys-area airport commissioner; the Port's waterfront investment is a policy, not a Charter requirement.
contests.yesMeans: The changes above become part of the Charter.
contests.noMeans: Current lease limits, commission makeup and Port practices stay as they are.
pros: Supporters (Councilmembers McOsker, Padilla, Park) say neighborhoods affected by airport noise and traffic deserve more seats on the Airport Commission.
Locks in the Port's waterfront investment in San Pedro and Wilmington.
Job-impact disclosure keeps automation and workforce effects in public view.
Longer leases can attract long-term private investment in infrastructure.
cons: No official opposing argument was filed. Residency quotas narrow the pool of qualified commissioners the mayor can appoint.
Longer 66-year leases tie up public land and limit future flexibility.
Writing the Port's 10% set-aside into the Charter limits how the Harbor Department can use operating income in lean years.
contests.fiscal: Mostly cost-neutral. Codifies an existing ~$28.6M/year Port allocation; applicants pay for their own job-impact studies.
contests.ballotSupporters: Tim McOsker, LA City Councilmember; Imelda Padilla, LA City Councilwoman; Traci Park, LA City Councilwoman

sources.label: LA City Clerk – Official Voter Information Pamphlet

contests.title: Half-cent sales tax for the LA Fire Department (citizen initiative)
contests.summary: Adds a 0.5% sales tax in the City of LA (raising the rate from 10.25% to 10.75%) dedicated to the Fire Department: hiring firefighters, paramedics and civilian staff; trucks, ambulances, helicopters and radios; brush clearance and wildfire prep; and building/upgrading fire stations. Raises ~$345M a year until voters end it, with annual audits and a 5-member citizens' oversight committee. The tax can only be collected in years the City keeps LAFD's share of the General Fund at least at its 10-year average.
contests.currentLaw: LAFD is funded almost entirely from the General Fund through the annual budget. City sales tax is 10.25% as of Oct. 1, 2026.
contests.yesMeans: LA's sales tax rises by half a cent, with the money locked into a fund that can only be spent on LAFD.
contests.noMeans: No new tax; LAFD funding continues to come from the regular city budget.
pros: Firefighters say paramedic response often takes nearly twice the 4-minute national standard; FD would add at least 1,000 firefighters and paramedics.
LA's population has grown 50%+ since the 1960s while firefighter staffing hasn't — and there are fewer stations.
Money is legally locked to LAFD with audits, public reporting and citizen oversight; the maintenance-of-effort rule stops City Hall from swapping out existing funding.
Wildfire prevention after the 2025 fires: more brush clearance and modern water-dropping aircraft.
Even at 10.75%, supporters say LA's rate would be lower than Long Beach, Santa Monica, Pasadena and Burbank.
cons: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn. says it would be the third sales-tax increase in two years (after county Measure A in 2024 and Measure ER in June) — about $86 per resident per year.
Sales taxes take a bigger share of income from lower-income households.
Opponents argue the City has an $8B+ General Fund and should prioritize fire protection over things like the $2.7B Convention Center expansion or homelessness spending.
As a citizen initiative it needs only a simple majority instead of two-thirds — the "loophole" Prop 43 on this ballot would close for future measures.
contests.fiscal: About $345 million per year for LAFD, collected starting ~110 days after approval, until ended by voters.

contests.title: Binding arbitration for county public safety employees (county charter amendment)
contests.summary: Amends the LA County Charter so that when contract talks with public-safety unions reach an impasse, a three-member arbitration panel (one picked by the County, one by the union, one neutral) makes a final, binding decision on wages, hours and working conditions. Covers ~17,000 employees in 14 bargaining units: firefighters, sheriff's deputies, DA investigators, medical examiners, lifeguards, their supervisors, and non-administrative civilians in Fire, Sheriff and Medical Examiner. Also bars strikes by DA investigators, medical examiners, lifeguards and those civilian workers, and restates the duty to bargain in good faith.
contests.currentLaw: If negotiations fail, the Board of Supervisors can impose its "last, best and final offer" on the union.
contests.yesMeans: Contract impasses with these unions go to binding arbitration; the covered workers can't strike.
contests.noMeans: The Board of Supervisors keeps the final say and can impose contract terms after an impasse.
pros: Supporters (firefighter and deputy unions; four of five supervisors) say it "takes politics out of public safety pay" and puts neutral experts in charge of resolving disputes.
Unions say staffing shortages and competition from other agencies are causing burnout; fair, competitive pay helps recruit and retain first responders.
Supervisor Kathryn Barger called it "a long time coming."
Adds a no-strike guarantee for several job classes.
cons: Supervisor Holly Mitchell: "Arbitrators aren't elected" and don't weigh countywide trade-offs like homeless services, health care and capital projects.
Former County CEO Joe Nicchitta warned awards could strain reserves, increase pension liabilities and hurt credit ratings, citing Vallejo and San Luis Obispo.

Accountability advocates say it reduces transparency and democratic control over ~17% of the county workforce's pay, while the county faces federal health cuts, fire recovery costs and large legal settlements.
contests.fiscal: No official cost estimate. Covered employees are about 17% of the county workforce; the county budget is ~$23B. Future costs depend on arbitration awards.
contests.ballotSupporters: LA County Firefighters Local #1014; Association of LA Deputy Sheriffs; LA/OC Building Trades Council

contests.title: County Ethics Commission independence and community investment set-aside (county charter amendment)
contests.summary: Gives the County Ethics Commission and Office of Ethics Compliance (created by 2024's Measure G) firmer independence: power to investigate county officials, candidates, lobbyists and contractors, issue subpoenas and fine up to $15,000 per violation, with a guaranteed minimum budget (~$14.3M/yr) and rules on appointments, qualifications and terms. Also restores the requirement that 10% of locally generated unrestricted county revenue go to community investment and alternatives to incarceration — the Measure J (2020) rule that was accidentally deleted by Measure G.
contests.currentLaw: Measure G created an Ethics Commission, but its powers, budget and independence are not fully locked into the Charter. Measure J's 10% set-aside was unintentionally repealed in 2024.
contests.yesMeans: Ethics Commission independence, enforcement powers and funding are written into the Charter; the 10% community investment set-aside returns.
contests.noMeans: The Ethics Commission continues under Measure G's framework without these guarantees, and the 10% set-aside stays repealed.
pros: Supporters (League of Women Voters, CA Common Cause, CA Clean Money) say it creates LA County's first truly independent ethics watchdog with real enforcement teeth.
A guaranteed budget means supervisors can't starve the commission that oversees them.
Restoring the Measure J set-aside fixes an "administrative error" and honors what voters approved in 2020.
cons: The LA Daily News editorial board called the ethics changes "plausibly fine" but opposes reviving Measure J's mandate, which locks in 10% of discretionary revenue regardless of circumstances.
Budget set-asides reduce the Board's flexibility during deficits (Measure J itself was struck down once in court before being reinstated).
Bundles two unrelated issues — ethics oversight and spending priorities — into one vote.
contests.fiscal: About $14.3M per year for the Ethics Commission (≈54 staff). The 10% set-aside redirects existing revenue rather than raising new money.
contests.ballotSupporters: League of Women Voters of LA County; CA Clean Money; Supervisor Lindsey Horvath; CA Common Cause; AAPI Equity Alliance

contests.office: Governor
contests.note: Open seat — Gavin Newsom is termed out. Top-two general election.
contests.about: The governor runs the executive branch, proposes the state budget (~$320B), signs or vetoes bills, appoints judges and agency heads, and commands the state National Guard. Four-year term.

candidates.name: Steve Hilton
candidates.background: Born in the UK; former senior adviser to British Prime Minister David Cameron; hosted "The Next Revolution" on Fox News for six years; co-founded a political-tech startup in Silicon Valley. U.S. citizen since 2021.
stands: Taxes: eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 of income (his campaign's "Califordable" plan) with a flat rate above that; cut the gas tax in half.
Energy: increase in-state oil and natural-gas production, suspend some environmental rules and roll back climate mandates to lower gas and utility prices.
Housing: cut regulations for starter homes; cap government fees on new construction at $50,000; loan program for first-time buyers.
Homelessness: ban street camping and clear encampments.
Education: freeze in-state public college tuition; education savings accounts (school-choice).
End Medi-Cal coverage for undocumented immigrants; "clean up the corruption" in Sacramento.
criticisms: Becerra says Hilton's tax cuts would mostly benefit the wealthy, that his "math doesn't add up," and that they would drain money from schools — "you're going to end up with Trump results."
Becerra ties him closely to President Trump on immigration, AI, energy and voting. (CapRadio found no evidence for Becerra's specific claim that Hilton called ICE policies "perfect.")
Has never held elected office.
candidates.endorsements: President Donald Trump, California Republican Party, Nisei Farmers League.

candidates.name: Xavier Becerra
candidates.background: U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services under President Biden (2021–2025); California Attorney General (2017–2021); represented Los Angeles in Congress for 24 years.
stands: Declare a housing emergency to finance ~40,000 already-approved affordable homes and, during it, freeze utility rates and home-insurance premiums.
Expand down-payment assistance; ongoing state funding for rental assistance and homelessness services.
Health care: strengthen Medi-Cal and work toward universal coverage (he has moved away from promising single-payer in the near term).
Continue California's legal fight against the Trump administration — as AG he filed 120+ lawsuits against the first Trump administration.
Supports the clean-energy transition but says he's open to revising climate goals if they become unaffordable.

Axios reported that Biden adviser Susan Rice privately disparaged his management of migrant shelters; Hilton raised it in the debate.
CalMatters and CapRadio reported that he has avoided specific commitments on many issues, including energy costs and AI data centers.
candidates.endorsements: California Democratic Party.

contests.title: $11.25 billion housing bond (legislative statute)

contests.title: Increase the state's rainy day fund (legislative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Raises the cap on California's Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund) from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes; requires bigger deposits in capital-gains boom years; exempts those deposits from the state spending (Gann) limit until withdrawn; extends required debt paydowns; and allows using revenue to pay down the state's ~$20B federal unemployment-insurance debt.
contests.currentLaw: Voters created the rainy day fund in 2014 (Prop 2 of that year) with a 10% cap. Deposits count toward the Gann limit, which can trigger taxpayer refunds when revenue is high.
contests.yesMeans: The state can save up to twice as much in reserves for downturns.
contests.noMeans: The 10% cap and current rules stay.
pros: Supporters say California's revenue swings with the stock market; bigger reserves would cover about half of future shortfalls instead of about a third.
Reduces boom-bust budgeting that forces cuts to schools, health care and public safety in recessions.
Backed by firefighters and the LA Chamber of Commerce as well as Democratic leaders; the Legislative Analyst has recommended larger reserves.
cons: Opponents (Reform California, many legislative Republicans) say reserves can become a political "slush fund."
Exempting deposits from the Gann limit lets the state keep more tax revenue instead of triggering refunds to taxpayers.
Money parked in reserves isn't available for current needs.
contests.fiscal: State budget reserves would be higher.
contests.ballotSupporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel

contests.title: Make the high-income tax permanent (initiative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Makes permanent the extra income tax rates on individuals earning over ~$371,000 (adjusted for inflation) — top rates of 10.3% to 12.3% — that voters first approved in 2012 (Prop 30) and extended in 2016 (Prop 55). Revenue continues to go mainly to K-12 schools and community colleges, with some to health care.
contests.currentLaw: These rates are temporary and, per the ballot label, scheduled to expire in 2031.
contests.yesMeans: The high-income tax rates continue indefinitely.
contests.noMeans: The rates expire as scheduled, cutting taxes for high earners.
pros: Supporters (CA Teachers Assn., State PTA, school nurses) say it brings in $5–15B a year for schools and health care, and losing it would mean layoffs and program cuts.
Doesn't raise anyone's taxes — it keeps current rates.
Avoids a budget cliff when the rates expire.
cons: Opponents (CalTax, Family Business Assn., Hispanic Chambers) say California already has the highest top income-tax rate in the nation and that this could push high earners and businesses out of state.
Makes a "temporary" tax permanent after voters were twice told it was temporary.
Ties the budget more to volatile high-income/capital-gains revenue; GrowSF notes only part of the money ends up in classrooms.
contests.fiscal: Maintains $5B–$15B in annual state income tax revenue that would otherwise expire.
contests.ballotSupporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
contests.ballotOpponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce

contests.title: Allow public financing of election campaigns (legislative statute)
contests.summary: Repeals California's 1988 ban on public funding of political campaigns, so the state and local governments may (but don't have to) create programs such as matching funds for small donations. Programs can't use money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety.
contests.currentLaw: Public campaign financing is banned statewide except in charter cities (LA and San Francisco already run programs).
contests.yesMeans: State and general-law local governments are allowed to create public financing programs.
contests.noMeans: The ban stays in place.
pros: Supporters (League of Women Voters, CA Nurses, Common Cause) say public financing reduces the influence of big donors and special interests.
Lets candidates without wealthy backers compete and empowers small donors.
LA and SF already use such programs; this lets other cities and the state choose to.
cons: Opponents (CalTax, Howard Jarvis, Family Business Assn., United Latinos Action) say taxpayers would be forced to fund candidates they disagree with.
Could direct money to fringe or fraudulent candidates.
Setting up and running programs costs state and local governments money.
contests.fiscal: Ongoing state cost of a few hundred thousand dollars a year for the Fair Political Practices Commission; any program costs depend on future decisions.
contests.ballotSupporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog
contests.ballotOpponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action

contests.title: Change the recall process for statewide officers (legislative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Ends the two-question recall ballot for statewide officers. Voters would decide only whether to remove the official. If recalled, the office is filled by the line of succession (e.g., the Lieutenant Governor becomes governor) or by appointment, or by a later special election — and the recalled official could run in that later election.
contests.currentLaw: Voters answer two questions at once: recall yes/no, and who should replace the official. A replacement can win with a small plurality (as in 2003, when Arnold Schwarzenegger replaced Gray Davis).
contests.yesMeans: Recalls become a single yes/no question; vacancies are filled by succession, appointment or later election.
contests.noMeans: The current recall-and-replace ballot stays.
pros: Supporters (Secretary of State Weber, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party) say a recall should be about whether the official should go — not a contest a replacement can win with a small fraction of votes.
Reduces "political gamesmanship" seen in the 2003 and 2021 recalls.
Authored by a senator who was himself recalled in 2018.
cons: Opponents (CA Republican Party, Election Integrity Project, Reform California) say having the Lieutenant Governor — usually of the same party — automatically take over would discourage recalls and protect incumbents.
Weakens a tool voters have used to hold officials accountable.
contests.fiscal: Net effect unknown; in a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars depending on the office.
contests.ballotSupporters: None submitted
contests.otherSupport: Secretary of State Shirley Weber, CA Common Cause, League of Women Voters, CA Democratic Party, Sacramento Bee
contests.otherOppose: CA Republican Party, Election Integrity Project California, Reform California

contests.title: $25 billion loan program for middle-income buyers of new homes (initiative statute)
contests.summary: Lets the California Housing Finance Agency issue up to $25B in bonds to offer fixed-rate second mortgages covering up to 17% of the price of a newly built home priced below ~$1.5M. Buyers must be California residents who live in the home, meet income limits (up to ~200% of area median income) and put at least 3% down. Bonds are repaid from borrowers' mortgage payments, not the state General Fund. Includes an optional builder track tied to labor standards and construction-defect rule changes.
contests.currentLaw: No state program like this; buyers typically need large down payments or private mortgage insurance.
contests.yesMeans: CalHFA can create the new-home loan program and borrow up to $25B to fund it.
contests.noMeans: No new program or bonds.
pros: Supporters (Realtors, carpenters' union, United Nurses, Treasurer Fiona Ma) say it puts homeownership within reach of the middle class "without costing taxpayers a dime."
Limited to new construction, so it should encourage more building instead of bidding up existing homes.
The Legislative Analyst estimates no direct state or local costs.
cons: Opponents (League of Women Voters, Reform California) say the state shouldn't be in the mortgage business and that it doesn't address the underlying causes of high housing costs.
Some opponents worry it enables deeper consumer debt (as little as 3% down) without solving underlying affordability problems.
contests.fiscal: No direct state or local costs; bonds repaid by borrowers' mortgage payments.
contests.ballotSupporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma
contests.otherSupport: California Association of Realtors, SEIU, CA Democratic Party, Sacramento Bee
contests.otherOppose: League of Women Voters, Reform California

contests.title: $8.4 billion bond for immunology research (initiative statute)
contests.summary: Authorizes $8.4B in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research: half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit research institute, half to competitive grants. $4.2B is earmarked for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Drugs developed must be offered to Californians at a 20% discount, and 10% of drug revenues return to the state.
contests.currentLaw: No dedicated state immunology research fund. (Similar model: the stem-cell institute created by Props 71 in 2004 and 14 in 2020.)
contests.yesMeans: The state borrows $8.4B for immunology research grants and the UC-affiliated institute.
contests.noMeans: No new research bond.
pros: Supporters (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's LA, Kidney Cancer Assn., nurses) say most diseases involve the immune system and immunotherapy holds huge promise for cures.
Backfills federal research cuts proposed by the Trump administration.
Drug discounts and revenue-sharing could offset some costs.
cons: Critics (Stanford's Robert Kaplan, League of Women Voters, OC Register) say it targets one narrow slice of research instead of a broad range.
Half the money goes to one institute; GrowSF reports the criteria closely match UCLA's existing institute, and the measure is bankrolled by philanthropist Gary Michelson.
Adds $500–600M a year in debt payments for about 20 years; research may not yield marketable drugs.
contests.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500M–$600M annually for about 20 years to repay the bond, possibly offset if funded research generates revenue.
contests.ballotSupporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer's Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc/CA
contests.otherSupport: City of Hope, American Association of Immunologists, CA Democratic Party
contests.otherOppose: League of Women Voters, Orange County Register editorial board

contests.title: Require government ID to vote (initiative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Requires voters to show government-issued identification to vote in person, and requires mail voters to write the last four digits of a government ID number on their ballot envelope — mail ballots without it would be invalid. Also calls for citizenship verification for voter registration.
contests.currentLaw: Voters provide a driver's license/ID number or last four of their Social Security number when registering; ID isn't generally required at the polls; mail ballots are verified by signature.
contests.yesMeans: ID requirements apply to in-person and mail voting.
contests.noMeans: Current voting and verification rules stay.
pros: Supporters (CA Republican Party, Howard Jarvis, The Transparency Foundation, Latino American Political Assn.) say ID requirements strengthen trust in elections.
Most states require some form of voter ID.
Adds a check beyond signature matching for mail ballots.
cons: Opponents (ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters) say it would block eligible voters who lack a license or documents — disproportionately people with disabilities, low-income and recently moved voters.
Mail ballots missing the ID digits would be thrown out, which could disqualify many valid votes.
Costs tens to hundreds of millions per year; the citizenship-check provision likely faces federal legal challenges.
contests.fiscal: Costs of tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement.
contests.ballotSupporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women's Leadership Assn
contests.ballotOpponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
contests.otherSupport: CA Republican Party, Reform California, Richard Uihlein

contests.title: One-time 5% tax on billionaires (initiative constitutional amendment and statute)
contests.summary: Imposes a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California residents with assets over $1 billion (roughly 200 people), payable over several years. About 90% of revenue goes to health care (to offset federal Medicaid cuts) and the rest to education and food assistance. The revenue is exempt from school-funding and spending-limit formulas.
contests.currentLaw: California has no wealth tax; it taxes income, including realized capital gains.
contests.yesMeans: Billionaires pay a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, funding mostly health care.
contests.noMeans: No wealth tax.
pros: Supporters (SEIU-UHW, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Teamsters, AFSCME, CA Democratic Party) say billionaires gained most from recent federal tax cuts while Congress cut Medicaid, threatening hospitals and clinics.
Could raise tens of billions (supporters estimate ~$100B) for health care without touching anyone else.
One-time tax limits long-term economic effects.
cons: Opponents (Business Roundtable, CA Medical Assn., CTA, Planned Parenthood, firefighters, Ron Conway, Chris Larsen) say billionaires will leave or have already left, shrinking future income-tax revenue.
Valuing private companies and assets is hard and invites litigation; constitutional challenges are expected.
Some health and education groups say they were shut out of drafting and that it doesn't fix structural health funding problems.
contests.fiscal: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars over several years; possible ongoing loss of less than $1B per year in income tax if some billionaires move away.
contests.ballotSupporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
contests.ballotOpponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
contests.note: Prop 40 contains a clause: if Prop 41 or Prop 42 passes with MORE yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void even if it also passes (and Props 41/42 contain matching language). Your votes on 40, 41 and 42 interact.

contests.title: Audits for new special taxes; count them toward the spending limit (initiative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Requires the state auditor to review programs before a new state special tax goes to voters (looking for ways to cut spending at least 10%) and recurring audits afterward. Any new state special tax enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 would count toward the state's Gann spending limit — nullifying taxes that exempt themselves, such as Prop 40.
contests.currentLaw: Some voter-approved special taxes are exempt from the Gann spending limit; there's no required pre-election audit.
contests.yesMeans: New special taxes face audits and count toward the spending limit; conflicting taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026 are nullified.
contests.noMeans: Current rules for special taxes stay.
pros: Supporters (CalCPAs, CalTax, CalAsian Chamber) say voters deserve to know whether programs are spending money well before being asked for new taxes.
Counting special taxes toward the spending limit makes taxpayer refunds more likely when revenue surges.
Accountability for programs that keep asking for more money.
cons: Prop 40's sponsor (SEIU-UHW) and Sen. Bernie Sanders say its real purpose is to "trick voters" into blocking the billionaire tax.
Backed financially by billionaires including Google co-founder Sergey Brin and Stewart Resnick.
Could make it harder to fund programs voters want through special taxes.
contests.fiscal: Net fiscal effect unknown; depends on future decisions by voters and policymakers.
contests.ballotSupporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association
contests.ballotOpponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
contests.otherSupport: Reform California, Sergey Brin, Stewart Resnick
contests.note: Prop 40 contains a clause: if Prop 41 or Prop 42 passes with MORE yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void even if it also passes (and Props 41/42 contain matching language). Your votes on 40, 41 and 42 interact.

contests.title: Ban new state taxes on personal property and retroactive taxes (initiative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Amends the constitution to prohibit any new state tax on the ownership of personal property (everything other than real estate — e.g., stocks, retirement accounts, business stakes, possessions) and any tax that applies retroactively based on past activity. Nullifies conflicting taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, which would include Prop 40.
contests.currentLaw: The constitution doesn't specifically prohibit a state wealth tax or most retroactive taxes.
contests.yesMeans: Wealth taxes and retroactive state taxes are banned going forward, and Prop 40 would be void if 42 gets more votes.
contests.noMeans: The state keeps the option to enact such taxes.
pros: Supporters (CA Professional Firefighters, State Building Trades, AMVETS, peace officers) say Californians shouldn't be taxed simply for owning retirement accounts, investments or possessions.
Protects against future taxes on unrealized "paper" gains, including in pensions.
Blocks retroactive taxes that change the rules after the fact.
cons: SEIU-UHW and Sen. Bernie Sanders say it's designed to protect billionaires and kill Prop 40, not to protect ordinary residents.
Permanently limits the state's options to raise revenue in a future crisis.
Major funding from billionaires including Sergey Brin.
contests.fiscal: Possibility that state tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
contests.ballotSupporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA
contests.ballotOpponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
contests.otherSupport: Reform California, Peace Officers Research Assn. of CA, Sergey Brin
contests.note: Prop 40 contains a clause: if Prop 41 or Prop 42 passes with MORE yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is void even if it also passes (and Props 41/42 contain matching language). Your votes on 40, 41 and 42 interact.

contests.title: Two-thirds vote for citizen-initiated local special taxes (legislative constitutional amendment)
contests.summary: Starting Jan. 1, 2027, local special taxes (taxes earmarked for a specific purpose) placed on the ballot by citizen petition would need a two-thirds vote to pass, the same as special taxes placed by local governments. Existing taxes are unaffected.
contests.currentLaw: Since a 2017 court ruling, citizen-initiated local special taxes need only a simple majority, while government-placed ones need two-thirds. (LA's Measure FD on this ballot is a citizen initiative under that rule.)
contests.yesMeans: All future local special taxes need two-thirds approval.
contests.noMeans: Citizen-initiated special taxes can still pass with a simple majority.
pros: Supporters (CalTax, Family Business Assn., Hispanic Chambers, Howard Jarvis) say special interests exploit the majority threshold, often in low-turnout elections.
Restores the two-thirds protection voters understood Prop 13 to require.
The Legislature placed it near-unanimously as a compromise to avoid a broader anti-tax initiative.
cons: Opponents (CA Professional Firefighters, CA Federation of Teachers, SEIU nurses) say it would make it much harder to fund local services like fire, schools and health care.
Lets a one-third minority block measures most voters support.
Takes power away from citizens who gather signatures.
contests.fiscal: Local tax revenues may not grow as much in the future due to the higher threshold.
contests.ballotSupporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
contests.ballotOpponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA
contests.otherSupport: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn., Reform California, Southern California News Group
contests.otherOppose: CA Democratic Party, SEIU Local 1000, Sacramento Bee

contests.title: Community health clinics must spend 90% of revenue on programs (initiative statute)
contests.summary: Requires nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics serving low-income and underserved patients) to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on "program services" advancing their charitable purpose, including patient care. The Attorney General would define qualifying expenses and could impose penalties on clinics that fall short.
contests.currentLaw: Clinics are regulated by state and federal health agencies but have no minimum spending ratio.
contests.yesMeans: Clinics must meet the 90% program-spending rule or face penalties.
contests.noMeans: No new spending requirement.
pros: Sponsor SEIU-UHW says clinics should spend more on patient care and less on executive pay and overhead.
With federal cuts expected to increase the uninsured, every dollar should go to care.
Gives the AG enforcement power and transparency over clinic finances.
cons: Opponents (American Academy of Pediatrics CA, school nurses, CA Academy of Family Physicians, CA Medical Assn., Planned Parenthood, clinics) say clinics are already heavily regulated and the measure is redundant.
Opponents estimate $1.7B in noncompliance penalties in year one, which could force clinics to cut services or close.
Clinics argue it's a union pressure tactic and possibly preempted by federal law; much depends on how "program services" is defined.
contests.fiscal: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees.
contests.ballotSupporters: None submitted
contests.ballotOpponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc
contests.otherOppose: California Primary Care Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA, CA Hospital Association, CA Democratic Party

contests.title: Speed up environmental review for certain projects (initiative statute)
contests.summary: Amends the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) for designated "essential" projects — including most housing, transportation, water, health, broadband, school and wildfire-mitigation projects: sets a 365-day deadline to finish environmental review, requires courts to resolve lawsuits within 270 days, and narrows legal challenges. Builds on the Legislature's 2025 CEQA reforms.
contests.currentLaw: CEQA requires environmental review of most public and private projects; reviews and lawsuits have no firm deadlines and can take years.
contests.yesMeans: Qualifying projects get deadline-driven reviews and faster, narrower court challenges.
contests.noMeans: Current CEQA procedures stay.
pros: Supporters (CA Chamber, Children's Hospital Assn., CA Water Assn., CA Council for Affordable Housing, CA Building Industry Assn.) say CEQA delays and "frivolous litigation" drive up costs for housing and infrastructure.
Keeps environmental protections but adds deadlines.
Faster delivery of housing, water and clean-energy projects.
cons: Opponents (Coalition for Clean Air, CA Environmental Voters, Physicians for Social Responsibility, National Wildlife Federation, Sierra Club, CA Labor Federation) say it weakens protections against harmful development.
Rushed reviews could cause poor planning with long-term costs to communities and taxpayers.
Up-front government costs in the high tens of millions per year, possibly over $100M.
contests.fiscal: Initial state and local costs likely in the high tens of millions of dollars, potentially over $100M annually, partly covered by fees. Longer-term effects uncertain.
contests.ballotSupporters: California Children's Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing
contests.ballotOpponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
contests.otherSupport: CA Chamber of Commerce, CA Republican Party, CA Hospital Association, CA Building Industry Association
contests.otherOppose: California Labor Federation, CA Democratic Party, CA Nurses Association, Sierra Club California, Clean Water Action
